prime.problem: The GPT-2 lecture is four hours of changes to one script: a module, checks, an init, a dozen speed tricks, a borrowed recipe and two scorecards. Without a map of the few ideas they add up to, it is easy to finish with a working train_gpt2.py but unable to say which line matters for correctness, which for speed, and which for the final claim.
prime.fits: This card spans the whole course and compresses its 15 cards into six claims. It leans on ideas from earlier courses you already have: the Transformer block from z2h-8, the expected initial loss and Kaiming init from z2h-5, and += gradient accumulation from micrograd.
expect: a module that matches OpenAI's checkpoint, checked by its logits
numbers you can predict before training: 10.82 and the one-batch overfit
speed as memory traffic, not FLOPs
GPT-3's recipe with a 2<sup>19</sup>-token accumulated batch, and the held-out scorecards
prime.goal: Draw the whole reproduction from memory: the module from ids to logits, the step-0 checks, one full training step, where each speed trick saves bytes, and the scorecards, and say for each line whether it serves correctness, speed or the claim.

attend: Why is loading OpenAI's weights into your own module a stronger check than counting its 124,439,808 parameters?
Which two numbers can you predict before training starts, and which kind of bug does each one catch that the other misses?
Why does the residual scale use √(2·n_layer) rather than √n_layer, and what would the stream's std look like at block 12 without it?
If TF32 makes the matmul arithmetic 8× faster, why does the step only get 3× faster, and what does that say about where the next speedups must come from?
Why does accumulating 32 micro-batches need each loss divided by 32, when clipping and AdamW would hide the difference in the step anyway?
Why is beating GPT-2's 3.2924 val loss on FineWeb-Edu weaker evidence than beating its 29.4% on HellaSwag?

must: Module names and shapes match OpenAI's checkpoint → the 149 tensors copy by name (four Conv1D kinds transposed) → logits agree with Hugging Face to 4.58e-05 → the architecture is proven before any training, and later edits are changes to checked code

An untrained model spreads its bets over 50,257 tokens → step-0 loss ≈ ln 50257 = 10.82 (lab 10.96) checks the init → a big model must memorise one small batch (10.96 → 0.36 in 50 steps) → that checks backward, zero_grad and the optimizer before any long run

Each Block adds to the residual stream twice → 24 independent adds and variances add → std grows like √24 → scale the two c_proj layers to 0.02/√24 = 0.00408 → the stream ends at 0.30 instead of 1.54 at block 12

The step is memory-bound (8× faster maths gave 3×) → the wins come from moving fewer bytes: bf16, fused kernels, flash attention never writing T × T, full tiles at 50,304 → 1000 → 93 ms on one A100 with the same loss → which is what makes a 10B-token run a ~2-hour job on 8 GPUs
elevated: backward() adds into .grad while the loss is a mean → accumulating N micro-batches without / N gives an N× gradient → clipping and AdamW's per-parameter scaling hide it, so only the printed loss and norm (N× too big) give it away

Val loss is measured on shard 0 of our own training distribution → it favours our model over GPT-2's WebText-trained checkpoint → the outside task (HellaSwag, completion-scored, ±0.47 points on 10,042 examples) is the fairer head-to-head
reference: config: 12 layers, 12 heads, 768 wide, context 1024, vocab 50257 padded to 50304 (124,475,904 params)
recipe constants: AdamW betas (0.9, 0.95), eps 1e-8, weight decay 0.1 on 2-D tensors, clip 1.0, max lr 6e-4, min lr 6e-5, warmup 715, max_steps 19,073

compress.prompt: Card closed, one sheet of paper: draw the course's whole pipeline from memory. Start with GPT-2's module from token ids to logits, then the two step-0 checks, then one training step from micro-batches to optimizer.step(), then the speed tricks placed where they cut memory traffic, then the two scorecards against GPT-2's lines. Label each part as correctness, speed or claim.
checklist: idx → wte + wpe → 12 pre-norm Blocks on the residual stream → ln_f → lm_head, with wte and lm_head one tensor
loading OpenAI's weights (by name, four kinds transposed) and matching Hugging Face's logits as the architecture check
step 0 ≈ 10.82 and one batch crushed toward 0 as the plumbing checks
std 0.02, with c_proj at 0.02/√(2·12) because 24 adds land on the stream
micro-batches with loss / N → grads add → clip to 1.0 → lr from warmup + cosine → one step per 524,288 tokens; DDP splits the micro-batches
bf16, compile, flash attention and 50,304 as fewer bytes moved (1000 → 93 ms), then val loss on shard 0 and HellaSwag vs GPT-2's 3.2924 and 29.4%

retrieve.q: Explain why this lecture can promise to beat GPT-2 when OpenAI never published how GPT-2 was trained.
answer: the released weights give fixed targets to beat: val loss 3.2924 on the same shard, HellaSwag 29.4%
the GPT-3 paper supplies a full recipe for a model of the same shape
the module is checked against the real weights first, so the from-scratch model is the same architecture
better data (FineWeb-Edu) lets 10B tokens pass GPT-2's ~100B

retrieve.q: Walk through one optimizer step of the final train_gpt2.py on one GPU at B = 16, T = 1024, from the first micro-batch to the weight update.
answer: each micro-step: next batch, forward under bf16 autocast, loss / 32, backward adds into .grad
after 32 micro-steps: clip the global norm to 1.0
set every param group's lr to get_lr(step)
optimizer.step() (AdamW, weight decay on 2-D tensors only), then zero_grad for the next step

retrieve.q: You have one afternoon on a rented A100 and can apply only two of: TF32, bf16 autocast, torch.compile, flash attention, vocab 50,304. Which two do you pick, and why?
answer: the step is memory-bound, so pick the tricks that cut the most traffic
the two biggest rungs: TF32, one line, 1000 → 333 ms (3×), and torch.compile, 300 → 130 ms (about 2.3×)
flash attention (130 → 96) and 50,304 (96.5 → 93) are smaller once compile is in
none of them changes the loss, so the choice is purely about time

retrieve.q: Your from-scratch run prints step-0 loss 24.0 instead of about 10.9. Name the most likely cause, and what the one-batch overfit test would and would not tell you.
answer: the logits start far too large: a broken init (the lab's ×10 logits gave 24.01)
check the std of every weight: 0.02, and 0.00408 on c_proj
the overfit test would still likely drive the loss down, so it can't catch a bad init
the 10.82 check catches init problems; the overfit test catches wiring and optimizer problems

compare.q: The z2h-8 GPT and GPT-2 use the same block: communicate, then compute, added onto a residual stream. What does this lecture add that the character-level GPT didn't need, and which of those additions are about correctness and which about scale?
answer: correctness: matching OpenAI's names and loading its weights, the residual-scaled init, tied wte/lm_head
scale: a 50,257-token BPE vocabulary instead of 65 characters, context 1024
speed: bf16, compile, flash attention, padded vocab, fused AdamW, DDP
recipe: GPT-3's hyperparameters and a 2<sup>19</sup>-token accumulated batch, judged on held-out data and HellaSwag

compare.q: Makemore kept activations healthy with gain/√fan_in init and BatchNorm. GPT-2 uses a fixed std 0.02, a 1/√(2·n_layer) residual scale and LayerNorm. What is fundamentally different about the problem each is solving?
answer: makemore: activations shrink or saturate through a stack of tanh layers → scale by fan_in, normalise per batch
GPT-2: a residual stream that is only ever added to → its std grows with the number of adds → scale the writers by depth
LayerNorm normalises each token alone, so no batch coupling and nothing special at test time
both check the result the same way: a step-0 loss near ln V (ln 27 = 3.30 there, ln 50257 = 10.82 here)

compare.q: micrograd's loop was forward, zero_grad, backward, update. Which of GPT-2's additions live inside that same loop, and which one is micrograd's += bug turned into a feature?
answer: the four steps are unchanged; GPT-2 wraps forward in autocast, and adds clip and set-lr before the update
gradient accumulation deliberately skips zero_grad between micro-batches so the grads add
because they add, each micro-loss must be divided by N to get the mean
the same accumulation is why tied wte/lm_head gets the sum of both uses' gradients

predict.q: You keep everything in the final script but switch the config to GPT-2 medium (24 layers, width 1024), same vocab 50,304 and same 2<sup>19</sup>-token batch. Commit first: what are the c_proj init std, the expected step-0 loss, and does grad_accum_steps change?
predict.answer: c_proj std = 0.02/√(2 × 24) = 0.00289 (the init card's table). The step-0 loss is still ≈ ln 50304 = 10.826, because it depends only on the vocabulary, not the depth. grad_accum_steps = 524,288 / (B·T·GPUs) doesn't depend on the model either, so it stays the same unless the bigger model forces a smaller B to fit in memory, which raises the number of micro-steps.

apply.task: Plan the real run on paper, using only the ideas on this card, then check each number against the labs. Compute: grad_accum_steps at B = 16, T = 1024 on 1 GPU and on 8 GPUs; warmup_steps from GPT-3's 375M tokens and max_steps from 10B tokens; the expected step-0 loss once the vocabulary is padded to 50,304; the c_proj std for 12 layers; and the M3's days for 10B tokens at ~1,300 tok/s.
apply.done: grad_accum_steps = 32 and 4 (big-batch lab); warmup 375e6 / 2<sup>19</sup> = 715.3 → 715 and max_steps 10e9 / 2<sup>19</sup> = 19,073.5 → 19,073 (optimizer-recipe lab); ln 50304 = 10.826; c_proj std 0.02 × 24<sup>−0.5</sup> = 0.00408 (init lab); 19,073 × 2<sup>19</sup> / 1,300 s = 2136.7 h = 89.0 days (results lab).
apply.hint: Every step covers 2<sup>19</sup> = 524,288 tokens however it is split. A token budget divided by that is a step count.
